items.title: Gul swoops late for buoyant Galatasaray to condemn Aston Villa to Champions League loss
items.summary: This was Aston Villa’s third trip to Istanbul in the calendar year but, this time, they departed with different emotions. Unlike on the banks of the Bosphorus at Besiktas Park in May, the scene of their unforgettable Europa League triumph, or at Fenerbahce in January, they came away with a bloody nose. Galatasaray’s match-winner, Deniz Gul, finished with similar, the substitute requiring a bandage after bravely taking a boot to the face from Nicolas Jackson as the hosts rippled the net on 77 minutes. It was the game’s first effort on target, Galatasaray maintaining their commanding form on home soil to extend Villa’s winless run to six matches in all competitions.On the outside, this is a gladiatorial arena, a giant spaceship parked on Ali Sami Yen complex. But inside there is a poor pitch that began cutting up during the warm-up. John McGinn, one of four changes from Villa’s ­stalemate with Sunderland on Saturday, gestured towards the turf in frustration after a through ball went awry, but nobody of a Villa persuasion could blame defeat on the surface. As Unai Emery had stated, it was the same for both teams. Continue reading...

items.title: The line between sports hero and gambling shill is fast disappearing
items.summary: For big stars, endorsing companies like Kalshi and Polymarket is just another day in the beautiful business of being – and staying – richWhen Giannis Antetokounmpo announced he was taking an investment stake in prediction market Kalshi in February, the claim he made to accompany the announcement – “We all on Kalshi now” – sounded as absurd as the howls of outrage from sports lovers seemed universal. Nine months later, Kalshi’s grip on American fans appears murderously tight: notional monthly trading volume on the platform, the majority of which is taken up by wagers on sports, increased to nearly $100bn in October from $40bn in August, as the company gears up for yet another funding round at a rumored valuation of $65bn ahead of a potential IPO. Rival prediction market Polymarket, which relaunched in the US late last year after regulators shut it down in 2022, has seen similar growth over recent months. However righteous the disgust from fans on social media at the deepening incursion of these odious platforms into professional sport may be, their popularity seems only to grow.More perplexing is the widening circle of athletes like Giannis who’ve thrown off whatever shame might once have come from association with these businesses and given them their full-throated support. The line between role model and shill in professional sports is now essentially non-existent. Pete Sampras, a man so private in retirement it can often seem like his entire tennis career was a collective hallucination, released an ad for Kalshi during this year’s US Open after two decades largely out of the public eye. José Mourinho trousered a brick of Kalshi cash this summer in exchange for a gambling promo during the World Cup. The prediction market machine now sponsors Jalen Brunson and Josh Hart’s Roommates Show, on which the recently crowned pair of NBA champions begin every episode dutifully informing us that their amazingly dreary podcast is “presented by Polymarket, the top prediction market”. LeBron James will make more from his recently announced partnership with Polymarket – $15m a year – than he will from playing for the Philadelphia 76ers. Somehow we’ve arrived at the point where it’s bigger news if a professional athlete takes a firm stand against the prediction markets, as Victor Wembanyama recently did, rather than pockets the cash to endorse them.
